source_text: Ἀπὸ δὲ τούτων ἁπασῶν ἐμαυτὸν ἐπιστρέψας τῶν ἐννοιῶν κατεσκεψάμην καὶ ἀπεστράφην πάντα εἴδη συκοφαντιῶν τὰ ἐν ἀνθρώποις πλαζόμενα, ἐξ ὧν τινὲς μὲν ἀδικούμενοι δακρύουσι καὶ θρηνοῦσι, βίᾳ καταβεβλημένοι τῶν ἐπαμυνόντων, ἢ ὅλως παραμυθησομένων αὐτοὺς πάσης πανταχόθεν κατεχούσης ἀπορίας· οἱ δὲ χειροδίκαι εἰς ὕψος αἴρονται, ἐξ οὗ καὶ πεσοῦνται. Τῶν δὲ ἀδίκων καὶ θρασέων, οἱ μὲν ἀποθανόντες, ἄμεινον παρὰ τοὺς μέχρι νῦν ζῶντας ἔπραξαν. Αἱρετώτερος δὲ τούτων ἀμφοτέρων, ὁ ὅμοιος αὐτοῖς ἐσόμενος, μηδέπω δὲ γεγονώς, ὅτι οὔπω τῆς κατὰ ἀνθρώπους ἥψατο πονηρίας. Φανερὸν δέ μοι ἐγένετο καὶ ὁπόσος ἀνδρὶ φθόνος παρὰ τῶν πέλας ἕπεται, οἶστρος ὑπάρχων πονηροῦ πνεύματος· καὶ ὅτι ὁ ὑποδεξάμενός τε αὐτόν, καὶ οἱονεὶ προστερνισάμενος, οὐδὲν ἕτερον ἔχει, ἢ τὸ διεσθίειν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχήν, καὶ διαπρίειν τε καὶ δαπανᾶν μετὰ τοῦ σώματος ἑαυτοῦ λύπην ἀπαραμύθητον, τὴν τῶν ἄλλων εὐπραγίαν τιθέμενον. Ἕλοιτο δ᾽ ἄν τις εὖ φρονῶν θατέραν ἐμπλῆσαι τῶν χειρῶν, σὺν ῥᾳστώνῃ καὶ πραότητι, ἤπερ ἀμφοτέρας σὺν μόχθῳ, καὶ δολεροῦ πνεύματος πανουργίᾳ. Ἔστι δέ τι καὶ ἕτερον, ὅπερ οἶδα συμβαῖνον παρὰ τὸ προσῆκον, ἀνδρὸς ἕνεκα προαιρέσεως οὐκ ἀγαθῆς. Ὃς μεμονωμένος πάντοθεν, καὶ οὔτε ἀδελφὸν ἔχων, οὔτε υἱόν, κτήμασι δὲ πολλοῖς εὐθηνούμενος, ἀπληστίᾳ συζῶν, χρηστότητι ἑαυτὸν οὐθ᾽ ὅλως ὁτιοῦν ἐπιδοῦναι θέλει. Ἡδέως οὖν ἂν αὐτὸν ἐροίμην, ὅτου χάριν ὁ τοιοῦτος μοχθεῖ, τὸ μὲν ἀγαθόν τι δρᾶσαι προτροπάδην φεύγων, ποικίλαις δὲ τοῦ χρηματίσασθαί ποθεν ἐπιθυμίαις διασπώμενος.
thought_title: Oppression, envy and the lonely miser
orientation: Oppression, envy and the lonely miser show the wickedness that runs through human life.
pass_a_gloss: Having turned myself away from all these thoughts, I examined and turned away from all kinds of false accusations, oppressions wandering among men, from which some, being wronged, weep and lament, thrown down by force, complete want of those who would help or at all would comfort them holding them from every side; but those who do justice with their own hands are lifted to a height, from which they will also fall. Of the unjust and bold, those who have died fared better than those living until now. More to be chosen than both of these is the one who will be like them, but has not yet come to be, because he has not yet touched the wickedness among men. It became evident to me also how much envy follows a man from his neighbors, being a gadfly, goad of an evil spirit; and that the one who has received it and as it were clasped it to his breast has nothing else than to eat through his own soul, and to saw through and consume it together with his body, setting down the prosperity of others as an inconsolable grief. One being sensible would choose to fill one of the two hands with ease and gentleness, rather than both with toil and the knavery of a deceitful spirit. There is also something else which I know happening contrary to the fitting, on account of a man's not-good choice. Who, isolated on all sides, and having neither brother nor son, but flourishing in many possessions, living with insatiability, is not willing to give himself in any way at all to goodness. Gladly then would I ask him for what or for whom such a one toils, fleeing headlong from doing anything good, but torn apart by varied desires of making money from somewhere.

pass_b_english: Turning myself away from all these thoughts, I looked closely at all the kinds of oppression that roam among human beings, and I turned from them in disgust (Ecclesiastes 4:1). Through them some are wronged and weep and lament, struck down by force, while on every side there is no one at all to defend them or even to comfort them; and those who take the law into their own hands are lifted on high, from where they will also fall. Of the unjust and the reckless, those who have died have fared better than those who are still alive (Ecclesiastes 4:2). More to be preferred than both is the one who is to be like them but has not yet been born, because he has not yet touched the wickedness found among human beings (Ecclesiastes 4:3).

It also became clear to me how much envy pursues a man from his neighbors (Ecclesiastes 4:4), the goad of an evil spirit, and that the one who welcomes it and, as it were, clasps it to his breast is left with nothing but to eat away his own soul, to saw it through and wear it out along with his own body (Ecclesiastes 4:5), making the good fortune of others a grief past all comfort. A sensible person would rather fill one hand with ease and gentleness than both hands with toil and the cunning of a deceitful spirit (Ecclesiastes 4:6).

There is something else too which I know happens contrary to what is fitting, because of a man's will that is not good (Ecclesiastes 4:7). He stands utterly alone, with neither brother nor son, yet thrives in great possessions; he lives with greed for company and will not give himself to kindness in any way at all (Ecclesiastes 4:8). So I would gladly ask him for whose sake a man like this toils (Ecclesiastes 4:8), fleeing headlong from doing any good, and torn apart by all sorts of desires to make money from somewhere.
notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 4:1-8. 'Oppression' renders συκοφαντίαι, following the LXX of 4:1 (συκοφαντίας), where the word means oppression and extortion, not only false accusation. 'Those who take the law into their own hands' renders χειροδίκαι (men of violence). Gregory limits 4:2 to 'the unjust and the reckless' (the dead have sinned less than the living); the English keeps that limit. 'More to be preferred' renders αἱρετώτερος. 4:5 ('the fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh') is turned into the envious man eating away his own soul; cited beside that clause. 'Will' renders προαίρεσις, as in section 2.1. ὅτου χάριν may be neuter ('for what reason') or masculine ('for whose sake'); 'for whose sake' follows Ecclesiastes 4:8 ('for whom do I toil?'). No doubtful readings in the copy-text.
